articles.title: BJP fields Hardeep Singh Puri as its candidate for Rajya Sabha bypoll from MP
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Wednesday nominated senior leader and Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri for the Rajya Sabha bypoll in Madhya
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Wednesday nominated senior leader and Union minister Hardeep Singh Puri for the Rajya Sabha bypoll in Madhya Pradesh.According to an official press release issued from the BJP's central office on Deen Dayal Upadhyay Marg, the party's Central Election Committee cleared Puri's name for the Upper House seat."The Central Election Committee of the Bharatiya Janata Party has given its approval to the name for the upcoming Rajya Sabha bye-election 2026 in Madhya Pradesh: Hardeep Singh Puri," the statement read.The bypoll was necessitated by the resignation of former Union minister L Murugan, who vacated the seat on October 14. His term in the Rajya Sabha was originally scheduled to end on April 2, 2030.The Election Commission announced the schedule for the bypoll on October 22.According to the schedule, the notification for the election will be issued on October 26. The last date for filing nominations is November 2, while scrutiny will take place on November 3. Candidates can withdraw their nominations until November 5.Polling will be held on November 12 from 9am to 4pm, followed by counting at 5pm on the same day. The entire election process is scheduled to be completed by November 16, the poll panel said.Puri, a former diplomat who later entered politics, currently serves as a Union Cabinet minister in Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government and holds the petroleum and natural gas portfolio.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: A Georgia winery owner challenged rezoning of 114 neighbouring acres for dense housing over traffic, noise and runoff; an October 27 appeals court reversed a lower-court ruling in the dispute with Hall County
articles.summary: A proposed housing development can raise concerns about more than just the number of homes planned for a neighbourhood.
articles.body: A proposed housing development can raise concerns about more than just the number of homes planned for a neighbourhood. For a Georgia winery owner, the rezoning of approximately 114 acres of neighbouring land prompted fears about traffic congestion, noise, water runoff and the potential impact on his business. The dispute reached the state’s Court of Appeals after the Hall County Board of Commissioners approved the rezoning for a planned residential development. According to the court’s October 27, 2026, opinion, available on Justia in Hall County v. Faul, the appeals court reversed a lower court’s refusal to grant summary judgment to the county and its Board of Commissioners, finding that the lawsuit failed to meet a constitutional requirement governing such challenges.Rezoning proposal prompted legal challengeThe dispute began in 2024, when several property owners applied to Hall County to rezone approximately 114 acres from agricultural residential use to a planned residential development. The application sought to permit high-density housing on the property. Mark Douglas Faul, who owns Arrowquest Services Inc., operates a winery on a 2.21-acre property in Hall County. He joined other property owners in opposing the rezoning, which the Hall County Board of Commissioners ultimately approved.The opponents subsequently filed a petition in the Superior Court of Hall County seeking judicial review of the zoning decision. They named the county, its Board of Commissioners, several county officials and the owners of the land subject to rezoning as respondents. The petitioners argued that the development could harm nearby properties and businesses. Their stated concerns included potential losses in business income and property values, heavy traffic, noise, odours, mosquitoes associated with planned retention ponds, water runoff and intrusions on privacy.They also raised constitutional claims involving due process, equal protection and the taking of property without just and adequate compensation. They asked the court to reverse the rezoning, declare the decision void and issue temporary and permanent injunctions, along with awarding damages and attorney fees.Case returned from federal courtThe respondents initially removed the dispute to the US District Court for the Northern District of Georgia because the petition included claims under the US Constitution. However, the case was subsequently returned to the state court after the petitioners dismissed their federal constitutional claims. Back in the Superior Court of Hall County, the private landowners sought judgment on the pleadings, arguing that the lawsuit should be dismissed because it did not comply with a provision of the Georgia Constitution governing actions against state and local governments.The petitioners then sought to dismiss the county employees named in the case. The trial court granted that request and concluded that removing those officials remedied the problem with the lawsuit's party structure. However, the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners remained defendants. Hall County and the board subsequently sought summary judgment, arguing that sovereign immunity continued to protect them from the lawsuit. The trial court denied the motion, allowing the challenge to proceed. The county and the board appealed that decision to the Georgia Court of Appeals.Appeals court examined sovereign immunityThe central question before the appeals court was not whether the proposed housing development would cause the alleged environmental or neighbourhood impacts. Instead, the judges examined whether the lawsuit complied with the constitutional requirements for challenging government actions through a request for declaratory relief.The court explained that Georgia's Constitution provides a limited waiver of sovereign immunity for certain lawsuits seeking a declaration that a government action was unlawful or unconstitutional. However, a case relying on that provision must be brought exclusively against the relevant local government, and naming unauthorised additional defendants can require dismissal of the entire lawsuit.The judges noted that the petitioners had asked the court to declare the rezoning decision void. By seeking that relief, they were relying at least partly on the constitutional waiver of sovereign immunity. Consequently, the lawsuit could not continue while retaining the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners as additional defendants.Earlier dismissal of officials did not resolve the issueThe petitioners argued that naming additional parties was a procedural defect that could be corrected by removing those defendants rather than dismissing the entire case. They relied on an earlier Georgia Supreme Court decision recognising that such naming errors could be cured.The appeals court distinguished that precedent. In the earlier case, the plaintiff had sought to remove the individual defendants before the lawsuit was dismissed. In the Hall County dispute, however, the petitioners removed only the county employees while leaving their claims against the Board of Commissioners and the private landowners pending. The judges concluded that the petitioners had not corrected the defect. Because the lawsuit relied on the constitutional waiver but failed to meet its exclusivity requirement, dismissal was warranted.The Court of Appeals therefore reversed the trial court's denial of summary judgment. It did not decide whether the proposed development would cause the alleged traffic, noise, runoff or financial harms, nor did it resolve the county's remaining arguments. The October 27 ruling addressed the legal requirements governing the challenge, rather than the merits of the rezoning itself.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: MLC election results: Congress faces setback across 4 states; state-wise results and key wins
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Congress faced a major setback in the legislative council elections on Wednesday, failing to secure a victory in the seats declared so far
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Congress faced a major setback in the legislative council elections on Wednesday, failing to secure a victory in the seats declared so far across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra, even as counting continued in several constituencies.The biggest setback for the Congress came in Karnataka, where it failed to win a single seat despite being in power in the state. The BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats, with the BJP retaining three constituencies and the JD(S) wresting the Bengaluru Teachers’ seat from the Congress. The defeat was particularly significant for the ruling party as it lost its sitting seat in Bengaluru Teachers’ and failed to make gains in any of the three BJP-held constituencies.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP and Samajwadi Party (SP) registered wins, while in Bihar, Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj Party opened its legislative council account by defeating the Congress. The RJD also scored a victory in Bihar, wresting the Patna Teachers’ seat from the BJP.Counting for 28 legislative council seats across Uttar Pradesh (11), Bihar (8), Maharashtra (5) and Karnataka (4) began on Tuesday following polling on October 23. The elections were held for graduates’ and teachers’ constituencies, with results declared for several seats and counting continuing in others.Here is a state-wise look at the latest results and counting trends.Karnataka (4 seats): BJP-JD(S) alliance sweeps all four, Congress draws blankThe BJP-JD(S) alliance swept all four legislative council seats in Karnataka, dealing a setback to the ruling Congress. The BJP retained the North-East Teachers’, South-East Graduates’ and West Graduates’ constituencies, while its ally JD(S) wrested the Bengaluru Teachers’ seat from the Congress.JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated sitting Congress MLC Puttanna by 908 votes in Bengaluru Teachers’. Ranganath secured 10,810 votes against Puttanna’s 9,902.BJP’s Shashil G Namoshi retained North-East Teachers’ by 3,297 votes, securing his fifth victory from the constituency with 15,596 votes against Congress candidate Sharanappa Mattur’s 12,299.In South-East Graduates’, BJP candidate K M Suresh defeated Congress nominee Shashi Hulikunte Mutt by 23,098 votes. Sitting BJP MLC S V Sankanur retained West Graduates’, defeating Congress candidate Mohan Limbikai by 9,323 votes.The results marked a clean sweep for the opposition alliance, with the Congress failing to win a single seat despite campaigning by chief minister D K Shivakumar, former chief minister Siddaramaiah and other senior leaders.However, the results are not expected to affect the stability of the Congress government or significantly alter the balance of power in the 75-member Legislative Council.Uttar Pradesh (11 seats): BJP wins four seats, SP secures twoThe BJP won six of the 11 Uttar Pradesh Legislative Council seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured three, with counting underway in the remaining constituencies, officials said on Wednesday.The BJP won the Agra Graduates’, Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers’, Lucknow Teachers’, Meerut Teachers’, Meerut Graduates’ and Gorakhpur-Faizabad Teachers’ constituencies.The Samajwadi Party won the Allahabad-Jhansi Graduates’, Varanasi Teachers’ and Agra-Aligarh Teachers’ constituencies.In the Agra Graduates’ constituency, BJP candidate Manvendra Pratap Singh (Guruji) was declared elected.The BJP retained the Bareilly-Moradabad Teachers’ seat, with its candidate Hari Singh Dhillon defeating SP nominee Danish Akhtar by 17,676 votes. Dhillon secured 21,672 votes against Akhtar’s 3,996 after all five rounds of counting.The BJP also won the Lucknow Teachers’ constituency, where its candidate Umesh Dwivedi defeated SP’s Sushil Kumar by 6,992 votes. Dwivedi secured 13,179 votes against Kumar’s 8,371.In Meerut, the BJP won both the Teachers’ and Graduates’ constituencies. Its candidates Dinesh Kumar Goyal and Shri Chand Sharma were declared winners in the Graduates’ and Teachers’ seats, respectively.The BJP also retained the Gorakhpur-Faizabad Teachers’ constituency, with its candidate Dhruv Tripathi defeating Independent candidate Rajiv Yadav by 307 votes. Tripathi secured 14,887 votes against Yadav’s 14,580.However, Yadav alleged that the election had been manipulated to ensure his defeat. Claiming that around 1,000 votes had been stolen, he said he would approach the Election Commission and the court to challenge the result. He also demanded a forensic examination of 1,612 votes counted in the fourth round, alleging irregularities in the counting process.Disputes had arisen earlier over the vote margin and counting procedures. Candidates raised objections after 52 more votes were found in a ballot box from a booth in Mau than were recorded in the official data. Additional Commissioner of Ayodhya Ajay Saini was removed following a complaint by a candidate. The administration maintained that the counting was being conducted according to the rules.In the Allahabad-Jhansi Graduates’ constituency, SP candidate Mansingh Yadav was declared elected, while the party’s Lal Bihari Yadav won the Varanasi Teachers’ seat. SP MP from Chandauli Virendra Singh questioned the district administration over an alleged delay of around six hours in announcing the Varanasi result.In the Agra-Aligarh Teachers’ constituency, SP candidate Akash Agrawal defeated BJP’s Hari Kishore Tiwari. Agrawal received his election certificate at the counting centre in Agra on Wednesday.Earlier, SP president Akhilesh Yadav claimed victory and shared a video on X showing Agrawal wearing a torn kurta. His supporters alleged that he had been assaulted."Let the BJP explain how the treatment meted out by its people to SP MLC candidate, Akash Agrawal, who is winning from Agra, can be justified," he said.The former chief minister urged the Election Commission, the Supreme Court and the President to take immediate cognisance of the matter. He said society was deeply outraged by what he described as "inhumane treatment" and "violence" against Agrawal."Even the Agrawal community has now realised that in truth, the BJP is no one's ally," he claimed.The MLC polls are being viewed as a prestige battle between the ruling BJP and the opposition SP ahead of the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. Voting for the 11 seats, comprising five Graduates’ and six Teachers’ constituencies, was held on Friday, with counting beginning at 8 am on Tuesday.Bihar (8 seats): Jan Suraaj opens account, RJD defeats BJP veteranThe Bihar Legislative Council elections delivered several upsets, with five sitting MLCs losing their seats and the Jan Suraaj Party securing its maiden victory in the Upper House.Of the eight seats, which went to polls on October 23, the BJP won three, Independents secured two, while the RJD, Jan Suraaj Party and NDA partner JD(U) won one seat each.Jan Suraaj Party candidate Suresh Prasad Rai defeated sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha in the Darbhanga Teachers’ constituency, marking the party’s first win in the Bihar Legislative Council.BJP candidate Narendra Prasad Singh won the Tirhut Teachers’ seat, defeating CPI MLC Sanjay Kumar Singh, who had the support of the INDIA bloc.In another major upset, RJD candidate Sanjeev Kumar defeated veteran BJP MLC Nawal Kishore Yadav in the Patna Teachers’ constituency, ending the latter’s long hold on the seat.Independent candidate Rahul Raj also defeated sitting MLC Afaq Ahmed in the Saran Teachers’ constituency.Meanwhile, JD(U)’s Neeraj Kumar retained the Patna Graduates’ seat for a fourth consecutive term, defeating his rivals despite a challenge from within his party. BJP candidates Sarvesh Kumar and N K Yadav retained the Darbhanga Graduates’ and Kosi Graduates’ seats, respectively.Independent candidate Bansi Dhar Brajwasi also retained the Tirhut Graduates’ constituency, while two other seats went to the BJP and Independents as part of the overall tally.The Congress, which contested five seats, failed to win any and is now left with just one member in the 75-member Bihar Legislative Council.The polls saw 90 candidates contesting four Graduates’ constituencies and 60 candidates in four Teachers’ constituencies. The four Graduates’ seats had 4.92 lakh eligible voters, while the four Teachers’ constituencies had 40,253 voters.Maharashtra (5 seats): BJP's Sudhakar Kohale leads Congress in NagpurThe BJP-led ruling Mahayuti won two seats in Maharashtra, while the opposition NCP (SP) bagged two, as results were declared for four of the five Legislative Council seats.Shiv Sena candidate Kiran Sarnaik won the Amravati Teachers’ constituency, while BJP candidate Kaustubh Gawade emerged victorious in the Pune Teachers’ constituency.In the Pune Graduates’ constituency, NCP (SP) candidate Harshada Deshmukh-Jadhav won, while party candidate Pratapsinh Patil secured victory in the Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) Graduates’ constituency.Counting continued in the Nagpur Division Graduates’ constituency, where BJP candidate Sudhakar Kohale was leading sitting Congress MLC Abhijit Wanjari by over 4,000 votes after the second round.Kohale secured 60,924 votes against Wanjari’s 56,630, while Independent candidate Nitesh Karale received 24,249 votes. A total of 15,106 votes were declared invalid.None of the candidates had reached the winning quota of 75,438 votes, leaving the final outcome dependent on further counting and the transfer of preferential votes.The polls, held on October 23, saw 182 candidates contesting across three Graduates’ and two Teachers’ constituencies. The results are being watched amid rebel candidates, alliance differences and efforts by the BJP-led Mahayuti and the opposition Maha Vikas Aghadi to consolidate support.The terms of the sitting members are due to end on December 6, and the election process is scheduled to be completed by October 31.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Sweeping machine runs 56.5km in Gurgaon, sweeps 0.3km
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A mechanised road-sweeping machine (MRSM) in Gurgaon covered 56.5km in a day.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A mechanised road-sweeping machine (MRSM) in Gurgaon covered 56.5km in a day. That should have been great news, but the integrated command and control centre at Commission for Air Quality Management (CAQM) thought it was too good to be true. And it was.A detailed analysis found that the machine had swept just 0.3km, and the remaining 56.2km of its sojourn was off-route. Besides, the strayer had sped through its work at 23.2kmph, much higher than the speed at which it should operate to sweep effectively.This is one of the finds of the command and control centre - known as Platform for Air Quality Vigilance and Analytics for NCR (PAVAN) - to track pollution-related activities on real-time basis across Delhi-NCR.Set to be operational soon, it tracks live feeds from construction and landfill sites, emissions data from industrial units through Online Continuous Emission Monitoring Systems, and daily satellite data on stubble burning.Centre has integrated data from 2,300 air polluting industries It also receives data from all 108 continuous ambient air quality monitoring stations operational in Delhi-NCR, monitoring the status of pollution-related complaints filed on an app and social media, the implementation of the state action plan, and data from brick kilns.The centre, which is set to become operational soon, will monitor compliance with pollution control guidelines from 8am to 8pm. When a violation is detected, CAQM will send alerts to Delhi Pollution Control Committee and the respective state pollution control boards to take corrective action.Union environment minister Bhupender Yadav will visit to review the centre on Friday.The centre also has integrated data from nearly 2,300 grossly air polluting industries, which is being monitored to ensure that the emission levels from any industry do not exceed standards.Drawing on VAHAN portal, the centre will provide data on vehicles across NCR by category and fuel types.As of now, around six members of CAQM track the data received at the centre on a real-time basis for 16 hours. However, after the centre becomes fully operational, nearly 100 CAQM officials will be given access to the data for analysing the sector-specific status. PAVAN is located at CAQM's office in Janpath."Currently, only the CAQM team has access to this integrated command and control centre. In future, it may be shared with Central Pollution Control Board, union ministry of environment, forests and climate change and state pollution control boards," said a senior official.Earlier this month, Delhi Pollution Control Committee launched a 24x7 command centre in Shastri Park which has AI-based analysis, live CCTV feeds, AQI data, GPS tracking of road-sweeping machines, and field-team movements on a single platform to tackle air pollution in the city.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: A Washington man rented an apartment beside a car-painting workshop where fumes made him ill; after a $95,904 damages judgment, an October 26 appeals court preserved $75,000 but overturned the extra damages
articles.summary: Paint fumes drifting into a rented home can turn an ordinary tenancy into a question of health, safety and legal responsibility.
articles.body: Paint fumes drifting into a rented home can turn an ordinary tenancy into a question of health, safety and legal responsibility. In Redmond, Washington, tenant Eric Christiansen said fumes from an adjoining automobile-painting workshop made him ill and left his apartment uninhabitable. A trial court awarded him nearly $95,904 in damages after finding his landlords negligent and in violation of state landlord-tenant law. However, the Washington Court of Appeals, Division One, partly revised that outcome in an unpublished opinion issued on October 26, 2026, which does not constitute binding precedent. According to the ruling available on Justia, the court upheld $75,000 for physical pain and suffering and emotional distress but reversed the additional treble damages and ordered further proceedings on attorney fees.Paint fumes affected the rented apartmentThe dispute arose at a garage property owned by Larry Searles and associated with 938 164th Avenue, LLC. The facility in Redmond contained two apartments and an automobile workshop where Searles repaired and painted classic cars. Christiansen signed a two-year lease for one of the apartments on June 15, 2020. The other apartment was rented to Marshall Johnson, who worked as an automobile painter in the workshop. Although the workshop had a ventilation system and a paint booth, fumes and airborne particulates frequently accumulated when Johnson carried out painting work.Christiansen noticed the fumes entering his apartment on multiple occasions and began experiencing illness, physical pain and distress. On August 14, 2020, he complained to Searles that the fumes were making him sick. Three days later, Searles told him he would not be held to the lease if he wanted to leave. Christiansen also contacted King County about the conditions. On September 8, a county code enforcement officer inspected the property and determined that it was uninhabitable because of paint fumes and particulates in the air. The officer also identified missing occupancy permits. Both tenants were subsequently evicted, and Christiansen struggled to find alternative accommodation, affecting his eating habits and access to his mail.Trial court awarded nearly $95,904Christiansen sued Searles and the associated company, alleging negligence based on a breach of the implied warranty of habitability and violations of Washington's Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. Following a bench trial, the court found the defendants negligent and in violation of the legislation. It awarded Christiansen $25,000 for pain and suffering caused by physical illness and $50,000 for emotional distress, bringing the negligence damages to $75,000.The court separately calculated his actual damages under the landlord-tenant law at $6,967.99. It trebled that amount, producing an additional award of $20,903.97. Together, the two awards totalled $95,903.97, or approximately $95,904. The court also awarded reasonable attorney fees and litigation costs, to be determined separately. Christiansen initially sought nearly $98,465 in attorney fees but reduced his request to $76,710 after conceding certain objections raised by the defendants.Appeals court upheld physical and emotional distress damagesSearles and the company challenged the damages award, arguing that Christiansen should not have received compensation for emotional distress without objective medical evidence of his symptoms. The appeals court rejected that argument. It explained that Washington law permits recovery for emotional distress accompanying a physical injury. The requirement for objective symptomatology, which generally applies to certain emotional distress claims without physical injury, did not apply in the same way here.The trial court had found that Christiansen experienced illness, including an upset stomach, after exposure to the fumes. Its findings also recorded his physical pain and emotional distress, supported by his credible testimony. Because those findings were not challenged on appeal, the appellate court accepted them. It concluded that the established physical illness meant Christiansen did not have to demonstrate objective symptomatology to recover the $50,000 emotional distress award. The $25,000 for physical pain and suffering also remained intact.Treble damages reversed, fee award sent backThe court reached a different conclusion on the additional damages awarded under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act. The relevant provision permits treble damages when a landlord knowingly violates specified statutory requirements, including conditions relating to the rental property's habitability. The appeals court found that the award could not stand because the statute required prior government notice that the dwelling had been condemned or was unlawful to occupy. Although Searles had avoided the permitting process during renovations, the record showed that no government entity had notified him of a relevant violation before he leased the apartment to Christiansen.The trial court had reasoned that notice was unnecessary because the landlord had deliberately avoided government authorities. The appeals court nevertheless reversed the treble damages award under the applicable statutory requirements. It also vacated the attorney fee award because the trial court had not provided sufficiently detailed findings and conclusions explaining its decision. The case was remanded for further proceedings, including a clearer explanation of the basis for attorney fees. The appeals court also denied Christiansen's request for attorney fees and costs on appeal.The ruling therefore preserved Christiansen's $75,000 award for physical pain and emotional distress while removing the additional $20,903.97 in treble damages. The fee issue remains subject to further proceedings in the trial court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Refrain from seeing ghosts everywhere': Nirmala Sitharaman hits back at Rahul Gandhi over Tata Group remarks
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Wednesday asked Rahul Gandhi to “refrain from seeing ghosts everywhere” after the Congress leader
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman on Wednesday asked Rahul Gandhi to “refrain from seeing ghosts everywhere” after the Congress leader accused the government of “criminally destroying” the Tata Group.Sitharaman’s remarks came after Rahul Gandhi questioned business leaders’ "silence" on the comglomerate in a post on X, amid a dispute over the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of Tata Sons.Also Read | ‘Tata is being criminally destroyed’: Rahul Gandhi targets PM Modi, Amit Shah amid boardroom feud“Being the LoP @RahulGandhi, I suggest you refrain from politicising every issue. Also, casually labelling commercial and legal matters as criminal is unacceptable,” Sitharaman wrote on X.She alleged that the Congress MP had “repeatedly decried” the successes of Indian industry and its entrepreneurs. The finance minister also accused the Lok Sabha leader of the opposition of now trying to “incite” business leaders to join him in “spreading distrust and toxicity.”Sitharaman further claimed that the Congress had “smothered” Indian entrepreneurs through its “stifling Licence-Quota Raj”, contrasting it with the BJP-led government’s approach of "supporting industry, encouraging investment and promoting economic growth."“For decades, your party had smothered the spirit of Indian entrepreneurs under the stifling ‘Licence-Quota Raj’ and inflicted poverty on crores of Indians. On the other hand, our government led by PM @narendramodi values Indian industry as a creator of jobs and a driver of economic growth. Our policies have been tailored to enable enterprise, support industry and encourage investment,” she added.Sitharaman urged Gandhi to “engage constructively” with the government instead of “casting baseless aspersions” to suit his “narrow political motives”.“The Constitution of India ensures justice to all its citizens and our Honourable Courts are entrusted with upholding it. History is witness to the shoddy manner in which you, your party and the PMs belonging to your party have demeaned the judiciary. So Rahul ji, refrain from seeing ghosts everywhere,” the finance minister said.Earlier in the day, Rahul Gandhi wrote on X targeting Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union home minister Amit Shah: “Tata is being criminally destroyed, and no business leader dares say a word. How long will you stay silent? Until they own you? Indian business is not Modi and Shah's plaything. You lack courage. We don't. We will ensure justice for these crimes.”What is the Tata Sons matterRahul Gandhi’s remarks came amid a dispute within the Tata Group over the reappointment of N Chandrasekaran as executive chairman of Tata Sons. Tata Trusts chairman Noel Tata has challenged the decision, alleging procedural irregularities and questioning the validity of the resolution.In an October 26 letter to Tata Sons’ company secretary, Noel Tata argued that the reappointment was invalid, citing the absence of a Selection Committee recommendation and the failure to meet requirements under the company’s Articles of Association. He also sought the board meeting’s recordings, minutes and voting details, and asked the company to inform regulators that the resolution’s validity was disputed.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: In 1969, Chicago soldier Frank Kowalczyk recorded a 43-minute audio letter to his mother from Vietnam, speaking roughly 8,600 words as helicopters passed overhead; 57 years later, the Smithsonian preserves his voice
articles.summary: In March 1969, a 21-year-old American soldier stationed in Vietnam decided to do something different from writing a letter home. Frank A.
articles.body: In March 1969, a 21-year-old American soldier stationed in Vietnam decided to do something different from writing a letter home. Frank A. Kowalczyk switched on a reel-to-reel tape recorder and began speaking to his mother in Illinois, sharing updates about his fellow soldiers, life in the Army, family gossip and his plans for the future. During the approximately 43-minute recording, he spoke more than 8,600 words, while the sound of a helicopter passing overhead captured the reality of a war thousands of miles from home. Fifty-seven years later, the recording is preserved by the Smithsonian’s National Postal Museum in Washington, DC.Kowalczyk, a US Army private first class from the Chicago area, was serving with Headquarters, 46th Engineers Battalion, 20th Brigade, at Long Binh Post near Saigon. He had bought the recording machine from another soldier and preferred speaking into a microphone to putting his thoughts on paper.“I figured I’d just sit down and instead of writing you a letter just make use of tape,” he said at the beginning of the recording, explaining that it would be easier because he hated writing. The museum’s catalogue describes the message as having been recorded over several sessions in March 1969. While Smithsonian Magazine describes it as a 43-minute tape, the National Postal Museum’s object record rounds its duration to approximately 45 minutes.What followed was not a carefully prepared account of military service, but a long, informal conversation with his family back home in Calumet City, Illinois.From family gossip to the realities of warKowalczyk’s recording moved between the ordinary details of life and the unsettling circumstances surrounding him. He asked his mother about his father’s work schedule, checked on his siblings and wondered whether neighbours back home had married. He also discussed his friends, his experiences in the Army and his frustration with the routine duties imposed on soldiers at Long Binh Post.The everyday questions gave the recording an intimacy that a formal account of military life might have lacked. He was not simply documenting his deployment; he was trying to remain part of the family life continuing without him.He also talked about the differences between life in Vietnam and the world he had left behind. He described the military routine, the weather, the food and his experiences travelling around Saigon and nearby places. He mentioned learning Vietnamese and joked about how difficult it might be to stop using the language after returning home.Yet the recording also contained glimpses of the war’s harsher realities. Kowalczyk referred to a fellow soldier who had bled to death in a bunker because help had not arrived. He expressed a preference for being assigned outside the main base, where he felt soldiers were treated with greater respect.The conversation was not a polished historical account, and its value lies partly in that informality. His remarks captured the concerns, frustrations and familiar routines of a young man trying to make sense of military life while staying connected to people he missed.The helicopter that brought the war into the roomOne of the most striking moments comes when Kowalczyk draws his mother’s attention to a helicopter flying overhead. “Right now in the background, you’ll probably hear a chopper flying over,” he says in the recording. He goes on to explain that helicopters passed over the area frequently throughout the day.For his daughter, Manda Kowalczyk, the sound has become one of the recording’s most powerful elements. Speaking to Smithsonian Magazine, she explained that the helicopter was a reminder of the distance between her father’s home and the place where he was serving. “These helicopters are not in Chicago. This is happening in Vietnam,” she said.Lynn Heidelbaugh, a curator at the National Postal Museum, similarly highlighted what the recording preserves beyond its spoken words. The helicopter’s noise is something a written letter could not convey, giving listeners a sense of the environment surrounding the soldier as he spoke.Kowalczyk also asked his mother to record a reply and send it back with news, weather reports or television audio. Hearing familiar sounds from home, he suggested, would be strange in the best possible way because such material was rarely available to him in Vietnam.How audio letters connected soldiers with homeAudio correspondence had become a way for military personnel and their families to exchange more personal messages during periods of separation. By the Vietnam War era, reel-to-reel recorders were increasingly accessible, allowing some service members to record their own tapes.The American Red Cross also operated recording facilities in Vietnam and the Pacific, while its “Voices from Home” programme helped families record messages for relatives serving overseas. Such recordings allowed loved ones to hear familiar voices rather than relying exclusively on handwritten letters.Military postal arrangements made it possible to send eligible personal recordings from designated areas without ordinary postage charges. The Post Office Department also used the “space available military” transportation programme to move mail overseas. Kowalczyk’s daughter knew about it but did not recall hearing it until it became part of the Smithsonian collection. For his daughter, however, hearing the tape offered a glimpse of her father as a young man, before she could have known him in the same way.She told Smithsonian Magazine that hearing his Chicago accent made his voice sound like home. The National Postal Museum now preserves the recording and makes it available alongside a transcript, allowing listeners to hear Kowalczyk’s words and the sounds around him.More than half a century after he pressed record, the tape remains a document of both military history and family life. Its significance is not only in what Kowalczyk said about Vietnam, but also in what he wanted his mother to know about home, his friends and himself. articles.summary: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Wednesday took a dig at Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar after the BJP-Janata Dal (Secular) alliance won all four seats in the
articles.body: NEW DELHI: The BJP on Wednesday took a dig at Karnataka chief minister DK Shivakumar after the BJP-Janata Dal (Secular) alliance won all four seats in the state’s Legislative Council elections for Graduates’ and Teachers’ constituencies.The Karnataka BJP used the viral phrase “DK, it’s done, bro!” to target the ruling Congress after the National Democratic Alliance (NDA) secured a clean sweep in the polls, winning two Graduates’ seats and two Teachers’ seats.In a post on X, the BJP wrote, “DK, it’s done, bro! NDA SWEEPS 4/4 Teachers’ and Graduates’ constituencies in the MLC elections!”The phrase echoes actor Salman Khan’s widely discussed post, “Sonam, it's done, bro”, during youth and student protests involving the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP). The remark later became a subject of online satire, memes and political commentary. The BJP has now adapted the line to mock Congress following the alliance’s electoral success.Meanwhile, Shivakumar said the Congress would respectfully accept the people's verdict in the Legislative Council elections for four seats, acknowledging that the party fell short of its expectations and would undertake a detailed review of the results.NDA calls victory a sign of things to comeThe elections covered 19 districts, spanning nearly two-thirds of Karnataka, including the home districts of chief minister Siddaramaiah and Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge.NDA leaders have presented the result as a sign of support for the alliance among teachers, graduates and educated professionals. They have also described the clean sweep as a preview of the political contest expected in the 2028 Karnataka Assembly elections.JD(S) state youth president Nikhil Kumar called the outcome a “historic 4/4 clean sweep” and accused the Congress government of misusing state machinery and power during the election.“A historic 4/4 clean sweep for the NDA in the Karnataka Legislative Council elections (2 Graduate & 2 Teachers' constituencies)!” Kumar wrote on X.He further claimed that voters had rejected the Congress government and said the result reflected the political mood on the ground.“Despite the Congress government misusing state machinery and power, the educated fraternity has rejected their misrule. Spanning 19 districts (nearly 2/3rd of Karnataka), including the home districts of the CM & AICC President Sri @kharge Ji, this ballot paper mandate, free of any EVM debate, reflects the true ground reality!”, he wrote.Kumar also linked the result to the next Assembly election, calling the alliance’s performance a preview of what could lie ahead.“This unified fight by the NDA is a clear trailer for what lies ahead in the 2028 Assembly Elections. A huge thank you to the voters, and my heartiest congratulations to the dynamic leaders and hardworking cadres of both @JanataDal_S and @BJP4Karnataka for this towering victory!”Yediyurappa congratulates winning candidatesFormer Karnataka chief minister BS Yediyurappa also congratulated the four NDA candidates who won the seats, naming Shasheel Namoshi, Dr S V Sankanoor, K M Suresh and A P Ranganath.In a post on X, Yediyurappa described the result as a mandate against the Congress government and an endorsement of the NDA’s politics under Prime Minister Narendra Modi.“My heartiest congratulations to Shri Shasheel Namoshi, Shri Dr. SV Sankanoor, Shri KM Suresh, and Shri A.P. Ranganath, the NDA alliance candidates who have achieved an unprecedented victory in the election to the four seats of the Graduates’ and Teachers’ constituencies in the State Legislative Council. This victory is a clear mandate given by the state’s enlightened voters against the ruling Congress party and an endorsement of the development politics of the NDA government under the leadership of Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Ji.”He also thanked voters, party leaders and workers from both the BJP and JD(S) for their efforts during the campaign.“The victorious candidates will work for the people in a manner befitting the trust placed by the voters. Congratulations to all the enlightened voters who reposed faith in and supported our candidates, and to the BJP-JD(S) alliance state presidents, all leaders, people’s representatives, and every dedicated worker who toiled day and night at the field level for this historic victory. My best wishes for the successful tenure of the newly elected legislators,” he added.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 'Commit to ballot paper': Congress dares PM Modi after his 'how many seats' swipe over MLC results
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday took a swipe at the Congress over its dismal performance in the MLC polls held across four states.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday took a swipe at the Congress over its dismal performance in the MLC polls held across four states. The grand old party which failed to win a single seat in the polls, hit back at PM Modi over his “ballot paper” remark and challenged him to commit to holding all future Lok Sabha and assembly elections using ballot papers.The back-and-forth began when the Prime Minister in a post on X, wrote, "MLC elections in 28 seats across 4 big states - Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra, Bihar and Karnataka. Elections held using ballot papers. Guess how many seats Congress won?"Congress Rajya Sabha member Pawan Khera hit back at PM Modi, asking him to demonstrate confidence in the BJP’s prowess by committing to ballot paper voting in all future Lok Sabha and assembly elections.In a post on X, Khera demanded the suspension of the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls and the restoration of 13.3 crore voters "deleted illegally"."If Narendra Modi is so confident that EVMs have no bearing on election results, let him prove his confidence in the BJP’s electoral prowess through action, not rhetoric," he wrote."1. Commit to conducting all Lok Sabha and upcoming Vidhan Sabha elections by ballot paper going forward. 2. Suspend SIR and restore the 13.3 crore voters illegally deleted from the electoral rolls. 3. Terminate Gyanesh Gupta. 4. Repeal the law that gives life long immunity to Gyanesh Gupta," Khera wrote.BJP national president Nitin Nabin also took a dig at the grand old party, saying the party would continue to struggle for survival under Rahul Gandhi's leadership. Addressing a gathering during the BJP's ‘Loktantra Bachao, Arajakta Hatao’ march in Delhi, Nabin said PM Narendra Modi would return to the Red Fort after the 2029 Lok Sabha elections.Nabin also accused the Congress of opposing the cleaning of electoral rolls because it was distressed by efforts to remove alleged infiltrators.“There are voters who have died but whose names remain on the electoral rolls. There are also people whose names appear in the voter lists at two places. There are crores of such voters whose names are registered more than once, while the whereabouts of many others cannot be traced. This is what is called a ‘ghost voter list’,” he said.The remark came after the Congress drew a blank in Karnataka, where the BJP-Janata Dal (Secular) alliance swept all four legislative council seats despite the Congress being in power in the state. The results also saw the Congress lose its sitting Bengaluru Teachers’ constituency to the JD(S).The prime minister's reference to ballot papers comes amid the opposition's repeated allegations of irregularities in electronic voting machines (EVMs) and demands for greater transparency in the electoral process.The Congress suffered its biggest setback in Karnataka, where the BJP retained three seats and the JD(S) wrested Bengaluru Teachers’ from the ruling party.JD(S) candidate A P Ranganath defeated sitting Congress MLC Puttanna by 908 votes, securing 10,810 votes against his rival's 9,902.The BJP retained the North-East Teachers’, South-East Graduates’ and West Graduates’ constituencies. The results came despite campaigning by chief minister Siddaramaiah, deputy chief minister D K Shivakumar and other senior Congress leaders.In Uttar Pradesh, the BJP won four of the 11 legislative council seats, while the Samajwadi Party secured two, with counting continuing in some constituencies.Bihar saw setbacks for both the Congress and the BJP. Prashant Kishor's Jan Suraaj Party opened its account in the state Legislative Council after candidate Suresh Prasad Rai defeated sitting Congress MLC Madan Mohan Jha by 324 votes in the Darbhanga Teachers’ constituency.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: How Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s donation helped a Nashville free grocery store resume support for families on its waitlist
articles.summary: Pop icon Taylor Swift, 36, and NFL star Travis Kelce, 37, exchanged their wedding vows in July this year at Madison Square Garden.
articles.body: Pop icon Taylor Swift, 36, and NFL star Travis Kelce, 37, exchanged their wedding vows in July this year at Madison Square Garden. Ahead of their big day, the couple spent the week giving back. They donated $26 million to 20 charities, the Associated Press reported. One recipient was The Store, a Nashville non-profit fighting food insecurity. Rising food costs had forced the store to pause the admission of new families, and around 1,000 households were still waiting for help. That’s when an unexpected email arrived with a donation they simply couldn’t believe!An unexpected emailBrittany Brown, The Store’s director of mission advancement, read the email twice before she believed it. It arrived in the days before Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding in New York, a week when the couple’s names filled almost every feed. The message was not an invite. In fact, it had nothing to do with the wedding itself. It was about groceries, waiting lists and families who had been asked to be patient for months. Brown, whose job also involves explaining the non-profit’s work to donors and keeping the shelves stocked, quickly realised this was not routine support. “I quickly checked my email and was blown away, just really blown away,” Brown told Channel 5 Nashville.Country star Brad Paisley and actress Kimberly Williams-Paisley founded The Store, which opened in 2020. It works like a regular supermarket. Families referred to the store choose the food that fits their needs, with volunteers helping them shop. The store goes beyond traditional food aid and aims for longer-term solutions, according to its website.The email and the donation came at a time when the store had paused the admission of new families. Grocery costs were rising, and 1,000 households were still waiting. Brown would not say how much The Store received, but she confirmed that the pause was being lifted. “With this gift, we’re now going to be able to unpause that pause,” Brown told the broadcaster.In a video shared on Instagram, Brad Paisley called the donation ‘transformative’. “We just wanted to take a second and say it’s transformative, it will feed so many families, and what a way to start a marriage. I’m so excited,” the country star said.Kimberly said they were “so, so grateful”. She also pointed out that food insecurity was at a 10-year high in the Nashville area, making the timing “just so critical”. She added, “We’re just really grateful for your generosity.”Brown agreed: “What a wonderful thing to be thinking of others during such a chaotic time of wedding planning.”A $26 million charity donationThe gift was part of a larger round of giving. Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce made donations totalling $26 million to charities ahead of their wedding day. The donations were spread across 20 local and national charities, according to Swift’s publicist, with many located in areas where the couple has deep ties, the AP reported. Nine of these were based in New York, ranging from the Food Bank For NYC and City Harvest to Musical Mentors, a non-profit that connects music teachers with students in need.The couple’s ties to Nashville are evident in their generous donation. The pop star has called Nashville one of her homes since she was a teenager. However, her gift to The Store is particularly close to her heart because of her relationship with the Paisleys. In 2007, when Swift was just 17 and promoting her debut album, she opened for Brad Paisley on his Bonfires and Amplifiers Tour. Nearly two decades later, the friendship remains strong. In fact, the Paisleys attended Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce’s wedding.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Indian-American candidates in 2026 US midterms: Key races, profiles, latest polling & what's at stake
articles.summary: The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation.
articles.body: The 2026 US midterm elections are shaping up to be a significant test of Indian-American political representation.Four Indian-origin Democrats — Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam — are seeking re-election to the House of Representatives. Meanwhile, Vivek Ramaswamy is locked in a high-octane race for governor of Ohio, and physician-turned-politician Amish Shah is attempting to capture an open Arizona congressional seat.Read also | US midterm elections 2026: Why it's a do-or-die fight for Trump & the Democracts - explained in 10 chartsThe contests extend beyond Congress. Indian-American candidates are competing for attorney-general positions, mayoralties and seats in state legislatures across the country.The elections on November 3 will take place against the backdrop of a closely divided Congress and a national debate over the economy, immigration, healthcare, technology and Trump's policies. The outcomes could determine not only which party controls Capitol Hill but also how much influence Indian-American lawmakers exercise in Washington and state governments.Indian-Americans in key congressional races1. Ro KhannaRo Khanna, one of the most prominent Indian-American Democrats in Congress at the moment, is seeking a sixth term from California’s 17th Congressional District, which covers much of Silicon Valley, including parts of Santa Clara and Alameda counties. He faces Republican Ritesh Tandon in the midterms, after comfortably finishing first in California’s June 2 nonpartisan primary with 62.3% of the vote. Tandon advanced with 14.8%.The district, home to major technology companies and a large population of technology workers, has consistently favoured Democrats.First elected to the House in 2016, Khanna has established himself as a progressive voice on economic policy, technology, foreign affairs and the role of American power overseas.Born in Philadelphia to Indian immigrant parents, he studied economics at the University of Chicago and earned a law degree from Yale University. Before entering Congress, he taught economics at Stanford University, practised law and served as deputy assistant secretary of commerce under President Barack Obama.He now sits on the House Armed Services Committee and has been an influential voice on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and semiconductor manufacturing to US competition with China.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Ro Khanna, Indian-American Congressman behind Epstein files pushKhanna has been a vocal critic of President Donald Trump, particularly over his economic policies, immigration crackdown and approach to democratic institutions. He has challenged the administration’s priorities on taxation and economic inequality, arguing that government policy should benefit working families rather than disproportionately favour wealthy individuals and corporations. His opposition to Trump also extends to the president’s use of executive power and his approach to foreign policy, where Khanna has advocated greater congressional oversight of military action and a stronger emphasis on diplomacy.At the same time, Khanna has sought to distinguish himself from the Democratic establishment by championing a more populist economic agenda, including investment in manufacturing, clean energy, education and healthcare.His views on technology, economic inequality and America’s global role frequently place him at the centre of the party’s policy debate.2. Pramila JayapalPramila Jayapal is seeking re-election from Washington’s 7th Congressional District, which includes much of Seattle and surrounding communities. She faces Republican Nirav Sheth in the midterms after dominating the state’s nonpartisan primary, securing 84.4% of the vote against Sheth’s 9.8%.The result underlined her strong standing in a heavily Democratic district, where she has built a substantial political base through her advocacy on immigration, healthcare and economic inequality.Elected to Congress in 2016, Jayapal made history as the first South Asian American woman elected to the House of Representatives.Born in India, she moved to the United States at 16 to attend Georgetown University and later earned an MBA from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, she founded OneAmerica, a Washington-based immigrant-rights organisation, and became a prominent campaigner for immigration reform and civil liberties. Her experience as an activist has shaped her legislative priorities, particularly on deportations, detention, family separation and pathways to legal status.Jayapal has championed Medicare for All, stronger labour protections, affordable housing, climate action and expanded access to education. She has also held leadership positions in the Congressional Progressive Caucus and serves on the House Judiciary, Foreign Affairs and Budget committees, giving her influence over debates on immigration enforcement, federal spending and American foreign policy.Read also | US midterms 2026: From immigration reform to $15 minimum wage, all about Pramila JayapalA vocal critic of President Donald Trump, Jayapal has repeatedly challenged his administration’s immigration crackdown, deportation policies and restrictions on legal immigration. She has argued that the administration’s approach threatens civil liberties and undermines protections for immigrant communities. Her opposition also extends to Trump’s economic agenda and broader use of executive power, with Jayapal advocating stronger social protections and greater accountability for the administration.Her politics frequently put her to the left of the Democratic leadership, although she has worked within the party to advance progressive priorities.3. Ami BeraAmi Bera, one of the longest-serving Indian-American members of Congress, is seeking another term in California’s 3rd Congressional District, which covers Sacramento County and surrounding communities. He faces Republican Robb Tucker in the November 3 midterm elections.In the state’s nonpartisan primary, Bera secured 34.3% of the vote against Tucker's 29.9%.His re-election bid comes as Democrats seek to regain control of the House, with the Sacramento region offering a test of whether his established local support can withstand the broader national political climate.First elected in 2012, Bera has represented the Sacramento area in Congress since January 2013. The son of Indian immigrants, he grew up in California and earned his medical degree from the University of California, Irvine. Before entering politics, he worked as a physician and served as Sacramento County’s chief medical officer.His background has helped shape his political identity as a pragmatic Democrat who emphasises healthcare, public services and evidence-based policymaking rather than the more sweeping economic agenda associated with the party’s progressive wing.Read also | US midterms 2026: Who is Ami Bera, Indian-American Democrat seeking re-election from California's newly redrawn districtHealthcare remains a central part of Bera’s political profile. He has advocated improving access to medical care, reducing prescription drug costs and strengthening Medicare, while also focusing on education, infrastructure, veterans’ services and economic development. His approach generally favours targeted reforms and bipartisan cooperation, positioning him closer to the Democratic Party’s moderate wing on several policy questions.Foreign affairs, however, have become one of his defining areas of influence.Bera has served on the House Foreign Affairs Committee and the House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence, with a particular interest in the Indo-Pacific. He has supported stronger US engagement with India and closer cooperation with regional partners, while emphasising the strategic challenge posed by China. His work has given him a prominent role in debates over US-India relations, regional security, intelligence oversight and the future of American engagement in Asia.4. Suhas SubramanyamSuhas Subramanyam is seeking a second term in the US House of Representatives from Virginia’s 10th Congressional District, which includes Loudoun County and parts of the surrounding Northern Virginia suburbs. He faces Republican Dave Beckwith and independent candidate Ahsen Mujeeb Malik in the midterms.The district, home to technology professionals, federal employees and government contractors, has generally favoured Democrats, but the Trump administration’s cuts to the federal workforce and changes to government spending have made these issues particularly consequential for local voters.Subramanyam entered Congress in January 2025 after defeating Republican Mike Clancy in the 2024 election. His victory made him one of the newest Indian-American members of the House. Born in Houston to Indian immigrant parents, he studied at Tulane University and earned a law degree from Northwestern University. Before entering electoral politics, he worked with technology startups and served as a technology policy adviser in the Obama White House. He was elected to Virginia’s House of Delegates in 2019, becoming the first South Asian American elected to the state legislature, and later served in the Virginia Senate before moving to Congress.His political profile combines technology policy, economic affordability and a focus on practical local concerns. During his time in the Virginia legislature, he worked on issues including utility bills, prescription drug costs, education and gun safety. In Congress, he has emphasised support for small businesses, infrastructure investment, healthcare access and protecting federal workers. His background in technology has also shaped his attention to the rapid expansion of data centres in Northern Virginia, where new developments promise investment and jobs but raise concerns about electricity demand, water consumption, land use and higher infrastructure costs.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Suhas Subramanyam, Indian-origin Democrat who served as advisor to Barack ObamaSubramanyam has been critical of Trump’s policies on federal employment and government restructuring, arguing that abrupt cuts and uncertainty can harm public services and communities that depend on government jobs. His district is particularly exposed to such changes because of its concentration of federal agencies, contractors and defence-related businesses. He has also advocated reproductive healthcare protections, stronger gun-safety measures and policies aimed at lowering household expenses.New entrantsAmish Shah is running as the Democratic nominee in Arizona's 1st Congressional District. He previously contested the seat in 2024, losing to Republican David Schweikert. Schweikert is now running for governor, leaving the congressional seat open. Shah won the July 21, 2026, Democratic primary with 39.4% of the vote, defeating Marlene Galán-Woods, who received 34.4%. He faces Republican Jay Feely, a former NFL kicker, in November. The district is competitive, making this one of the more consequential races involving an Indian-origin congressional candidate. A FirstStrategic poll conducted on October 1 found Shah at 44.4% and Feely at 41.6% among registered voters, with a margin of error of 5.4 percentage points. A forecast updated October 23 projects Shah at 63% to win.Read also|US midterms 2026: Meet Amish Shah, the doctor seeking a second shot at CongressPia Dandiya is the Democratic nominee in Florida's 22nd Congressional District, an open seat where she faces Republican Casey Askar. Dandiya won the August 18 Democratic primary with 68.6% of the vote, defeating Kaysia Earley. Askar won the Republican primary with 30.9% in a crowded field.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Pia Dandiya, Indian-origin Democrat running for Florida’s open 22nd House seatRitesh Tandon is the Republican nominee challenging Khanna in California's 17th Congressional District. He advanced through the June 2 top-two primary with 19,793 votes, or 14.8%, finishing behind Khanna. The district is heavily Democratic, and current forecasts show Khanna with a substantial projected advantage.Nirav Sheth is the Republican challenger to Jayapal in Washington's 7th Congressional District. He secured second place in the state's nonpartisan primary, receiving 21,282 votes, or 9.8%. Jayapal won 84.4%. Sheth's advance means the November ballot will feature two races where Indian-origin candidates are facing off from opposing parties.Indian-American politicians not on the ballot Raja Krishnamoorthi lost the Democratic primary for the Illinois Senate seat and will not be the party's nominee in the November Senate election. His absence removes a high-profile Indian-American candidate from one of the year's most prominent Senate contests.Shri Thanedar lost the Democratic primary for Michigan's 13th Congressional District and is not the Democratic nominee in the November race.Gubernatorial race attracting national attention: Vivek RamaswamyVivek Ramaswamy, the Indian-American entrepreneur who emerged as a prominent voice in the Republican Party during the 2024 presidential race, is seeking to become governor of Ohio, the state where he was born and raised. The Republican nominee faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician and former director of the Ohio Department of Health. The contest has become a closely watched test of Ramaswamy's transition from conservative political outsider to candidate for executive office.Born in Cincinnati to Indian immigrant parents, Ramaswamy studied biology at Harvard University and law at Yale. He made his fortune in biotechnology and investment management, founding Roivant Sciences in 2014. His 2021 book, Woke, Inc., established his political identity as a critic of corporate diversity initiatives, environmental, social and governance investing and what he considers excessive ideological influence over business.During the 2024 Republican presidential primary, he advocated cutting government bureaucracy, restricting federal spending and challenging established political institutions. Although he withdrew from the race and endorsed Donald Trump, his combative campaign style helped establish him as a nationally recognised conservative figure.Trump subsequently selected Ramaswamy to co-lead the Department of Government Efficiency initiative alongside Elon Musk, although he left before the initiative's major restructuring efforts as he turned to the Ohio governor's race.His gubernatorial platform centres on reducing government costs, deregulation, education reform and expanding economic opportunity. His political relationship with Trump remains a defining feature of his campaign, even as he seeks to establish an independent record as a candidate for state leadership.The campaign has recently been embroiled in controversy over an advertisement featuring Acton's estranged mother criticising her daughter.Read also | US midterms 2026: Meet Vivek Ramaswamy, Trump-backed Republican seeking the Ohio governorshipThe ad drew bipartisan condemnation, including from DeWine, who urged Ramaswamy to withdraw it. Trump, however, defended the advertisement and encouraged Ramaswamy to continue running it, while Vice-President JD Vance also criticised Republicans who opposed it. The dispute has sharpened questions about the role of personal attacks in the campaign and whether the controversy could affect Ramaswamy's standing with voters.Polling has shown Acton ahead, although the size of her lead varies. The RealClearPolling average for October 19 put Acton at 48.7% and Ramaswamy at 44.3%, while a Fox News poll conducted October 15–19 found a narrower 50-48 margin.Other statewide contestsNirav Shah, a physician and public-health administrator, is the Democratic nominee for governor of Maine. He previously served as director of the Maine Center for Disease Control and Prevention from 2019 to 2023 and as principal deputy director of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention from 2023 to 2025. Shah won Maine's June 9 Democratic gubernatorial primary with 26.9% of the vote.Aruna Miller, Maryland's lieutenant governor, is seeking to continue in office on the Democratic ticket led by Governor Wes Moore. Born in India, Miller immigrated to the US as a child and built a career as a transportation engineer before entering politics. Her career includes service in Maryland's House of Delegates and election as lieutenant governor in 2022. Miller's political position differs from that of a standalone gubernatorial candidate: the lieutenant governor runs on a joint ticket with the governor. Her electoral prospects therefore depend on the performance of the ticket as a whole as well as her own profile.Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-American Democrat Aruna Miller seeks re-election as Maryland Lt Governor alongside Wes MooreSaritha Komatireddy, a Republican lawyer and former federal prosecutor, is the Republican nominee for New York attorney general. She is challenging Democratic incumbent Letitia James. Her campaign offers Republicans an opportunity to contest an office that has become nationally prominent because of high-profile investigations and litigation involving major businesses and political figures.Read also | US midterms 2026: How 9/11 shaped Saritha Komatireddy’s legal career as she runs for New York attorney generalJosh Kaul, Wisconsin's Democratic attorney general, is seeking re-election.Nithya Raman: Running for Los Angeles mayorRaman is a Los Angeles City Council member and urban planner seeking to unseat Mayor Karen Bass. Her campaign focuses on housing, homelessness, city services and the cost of living. She has become a prominent figure in the city's progressive political movement.Raman advanced to the November 3 mayoral runoff after the June 2 primary. Certified results gave incumbent Bass 34.3%, Raman 29.0% and Spencer Pratt 25.5%. Raman's advance to the runoff turned the race into a direct contest between two Democrats.Read also | US midterms 2026: Indian-born Nithya Raman challenges LA mayor Karen BassA McLaughlin & Associates/California Post poll conducted October 15–18 put Raman ahead by 7.9 percentage points. An Impact Research poll conducted October 2–7 put her ahead by 10 points, while a UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies/Los Angeles Times poll from September 15–20 showed an 11-point lead.Raman's candidacy is significant beyond her own electoral prospects: a victory would make her the first South Asian woman to serve as Los Angeles mayor. Her campaign will test whether her progressive coalition can expand sufficiently to defeat an incumbent in a city facing persistent housing and homelessness challenges.(function(){function e(){window.addEventListener(`message`,function(e){if(e.data[`datawrapper-height`]!==void 0){var t=document.querySelectorAll(`iframe`);for(var n in e.data[`datawrapper-height`])for(var r=0,i;i=t[r];r++)if(i.contentWindow===e.source){var a=e.data[`datawrapper-height`][n]+`px`;i.style.height=a}}})}e()})();What's at stake for Indian-AmericansFor the Indian-American community, the November 3 midterms are about more than individual victories. They are a test of how far a once-underrepresented community has come in American politics — and whether its growing presence can translate into greater influence in Congress, state governments and the national debate.The stakes are particularly high for the so-called ‘Samosa Caucus’, the informal label for Indian-American lawmakers in the US Congress.Ro Khanna, Pramila Jayapal, Ami Bera and Suhas Subramanyam are fighting to retain their House seats, while challengers such as Amish Shah and Dandiya are seeking to expand the community’s footprint on Capitol Hill. Their outcomes will help determine whether Indian-origin representation in Congress consolidates, grows or faces a setback at a time when immigration, technology, healthcare, economic opportunity and America’s role in the world are fiercely contested.The stakes extend beyond Washington. articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in Miami after leaving Brazil following election defeat to Lula
articles.summary: Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has arrived in the United States.
articles.body: Brazilian senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost the presidential election to incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, has arrived in the United States.The 45-year-old landed in Miami, Florida, with his wife and two daughters, 48 hours after refusing to concede defeat. Bolsonaro secured 48% of the vote against Lula’s 52% and subsequently threatened to seek to “annul” the election results.Earlier, flight-tracking website Flightradar24 showed that an aircraft matching Bolsonaro’s plane landed in Guayaquil, Ecuador, at around 4 am local time before departing minutes later for Miami’s Opa-locka Executive Airport. It had not been immediately clear at the time whether the defeated candidate was on board.From Brazil to US via Argentina and EcuadorAccording to Argentina’s migration authority, Bolsonaro, the son of former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, entered Argentina at 10:50 pm local time on Tuesday with his wife, Fernanda Antunes Figueira Bolsonaro, and their daughters, Carolina and Luiza. They crossed via the Tancredo Neves International Bridge, a key border crossing linking Brazil with Argentina’s northeastern province of Misiones.“Those who did so possessed valid travel documentation and faced no legal impediments to entering the country,” Argentina’s migration authority said in a post on X.At 11:30 pm, shortly after clearing immigration, the family boarded a private charter flight operated by Baires Fly SA, which, according to its filed flight plan, was headed for Guayaquil, Ecuador.Bolsonaro’s move is likely to strain relations between a newly re-elected Lula and his Argentine counterpart Javier Milei, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. Milei had travelled to Brazil to campaign for Bolsonaro.Why Flavio Bolsonaro left BrazilBolsonaro is under investigation by Brazil’s Supreme Court in two cases involving alleged corruption, money laundering and tax evasion. The court had ordered him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports by noon on Tuesday. It remained unclear whether he had complied, though he reportedly also holds an Italian passport.The senator received the Supreme Court order to hand over his Brazilian passports on Monday, according to a video in which he recounted being served the notice outside the home where his father is serving a 27-year sentence under house arrest. Jair Bolsonaro attempted a coup after losing the 2022 presidential election to Lula.Following that defeat, the former president fled to Florida before returning to Brazil three months later.In a video posted on Monday, Flavio Bolsonaro said he was seeking to rally fellow lawmakers against his defeat to Lula. Bolsonaro had won the first round of voting but failed to secure the 50% of votes required for an outright victory, triggering a run-off that Lula won to secure a fourth non-consecutive term.Flavio Bolsonaro’s eight-year Senate term expires on January 31, 2027, after which he will also lose the special jurisdiction that allows cases involving him to be heard by Brazil’s Supreme Court.Trump backs Flavio BolsonaroMeanwhile, Trump remarked early Wednesday (local time) that he would “approve” of Flavio Bolsonaro coming to the United States, describing the Brazilian senator and his family as “fine people”.“The election was really strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Trump told reporters at Joint Base Andrews in Maryland after returning from a campaign event in Texas on Tuesday. He did not elaborate but made clear that he did not endorse the election results.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted Christmas trees and recycled them into mulch, biomass and other uses, while the 2026 campaign raised £1.88 million for charities and helped support local communities
articles.summary: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted real Christmas trees after the festive season.
articles.body: A UK charity collected 88,544 unwanted real Christmas trees after the festive season. It turned them into reusable mulch, biomass and land management products. The effort also raised a record £1,885,915 for local causes. Just Helping, the national group behind the yearly Big Christmas TreeCycle Appeal, confirmed in its 2026 impact report that this was the largest campaign in its 14-year history. The total raised is £345,000 more than the year before. More than 4,000 volunteers gave their time to clear trees from streets across the UK. Under the scheme, households book a collection for their used trees and give a voluntary donation. The trees are taken to local processing hubs. There they are chipped and reused instead of being dumped in landfill. Data in the charity’s annual report shows that 81.2 pence of every pound raised went straight to 70 lead charity partners. Most of these are local hospices that organise the collection routes in their areas. Another 5.6 pence of every pound went to smaller local community groups. Just Helping kept 13.1 pence to pay for operating software, logistics and future growth.Nationwide reach and local community fundingThe 2026 scheme grew to reach more than 12 million households across the country. That is 3 million more homes than in 2025. Local hospice partners received £1,479,271 to support palliative care and community health services. A further £114,675 went to 109 smaller community groups, sports clubs, youth groups and food banks. These groups provided volunteers, vehicles and local know-how during the January pickup period. Just Helping founder Nick Stammers praised the thousands of people who helped with logistics, drove vans and chipped trees in the cold. “Every year, I’m reminded that the true strength of the Appeal isn’t measured by the number of trees collected or the funds raised, but by the extraordinary people who make it happen,” Nick Stammers said in a statement with the report. “To every volunteer, charity partner, supporter and corporate partner, thank you. Together you’ve helped strengthen communities, protect our environment and raise vital funds for local causes across the UK.” The Christmas TreeCycle scheme began in 2012 as a small local project. Since then, it has raised almost £9 million for UK charities. It has grown into a nationwide environmental and charity operation.Environmental benefits of diverting wood wasteCalculations in the report show that collecting and processing the 88,544 trees prevented an estimated 1.4 million kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions. When a standard two-metre real Christmas tree ends up in landfill, it breaks down slowly and gives off methane. This creates about 16 kilograms of carbon dioxide equivalent emissions. Recycling the same tree cuts those greenhouse gas emissions by about 80 per cent, to around 3.5 kilograms. According to Just Helping, the carbon savings from the 2026 campaign equal driving an average petrol car more than 6 million miles. That is the same as going around the Earth more than 240 times. The shredded trees were made into woodchips for local parks, public gardens and community spaces. Other parts became biomass fuel for industry or were used in farm land management projects. To cut the carbon footprint of the collections themselves, the charity teamed up with corporate supporters to bring in electric vehicles. Healthcare firm Bupa sponsored 20 electric vans supplied by vehicle rental company Enterprise. These worked alongside fleet support from waste management firm Biffa during collections in Greater Manchester.High-profile support and future expansionThe 2026 campaign also got more public attention. Outdoor ads ran on 13 high-profile billboard sites in Greater Manchester and drew an estimated 12.5 million views. The appeal appeared on national television for the first time, when Nick Stammers was interviewed live on Sky News. Well-known figures also backed the campaign online. They included actor Mark Bonnar, TV presenter Alex Jones, former Strictly Come Dancing judge Dame Arlene Phillips and actor Lisa Riley. Just Helping said it plans to expand the scheme to more local authority areas and hospice catchments before the next festive season. Its goal is to make tree recycling available to more people across the UK.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
